messages.subject: Re: data set up and analysis
messages.body_plain:
Lisa, if you visit a point 3 times, you must pool the data for the 3=20
visits, and record the effort as 3.  So you'll have just one row for=20
that point.  You won't get good estimates by point, and nor will they be =

independent, which invalidates the regression you plan to do.  It is=20
better to model the counts by point, using a glm with a log link, and an =

offset to take account of detectability.  The following paper outlines=20
how this can be done, but Distance isn't set up to allow you to do this=20
I'm afraid.

Steve Buckland

Buckland, S.T., Russell, R.E., Dickson, B.G., Saab, V.A., Gorman, D.N. an=
d Block, W.M. 2009.  =20
Analysing designed experiments in distance sampling.   /Journal of Agricu=
ltural, Biological and Environmental Statistics/  *14*, 432-442.

messages.subject: Re: Line transects os point counts?
messages.body_plain:
Carlos:

All else being equal, line transect sampling is preferable to point=20
transect sampling if for no other reason than you are gathering data=20
while moving.  If there is a reason why you cannot gather data while=20
moving (rugged terrain, being swamped by detections, needing to=20
distinguish calls of multiple species) then you should use point=20
counts.  But there are challenges with point counts; namely the number=20
of animals available to be detected by you while at a point is small=20
near to the point and increases as distance from the point increases;=20
even if animals are distributed uniformly in the habitat.  This is=20
because of the geometry of a circle (area of a circle increases as the=20
square of the circle radius).

While not a study of raptors, you might consult a paper by Prof. Steve=20
Buckland who applied several sampling methods (including line and point=20
transects) to songbirds Buckland, S.T. 2006. Point transect surveys for=20
songbirds: robust methodologies. /The Auk/ *123*, 345-357.=20
<http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/stb/songbird.pdf>

messages.subject: Re: help me to study butterfly diversity .....
messages.subject_clean: help me to study butterfly diversity .....
messages.body_plain:
Agnes:

I suggest you have a look at this paper regarding density estimation of
butterflies:

Brown, J.A. & Boyce, M.S. (1998) Line transect sampling of Karner blue
butterflies ( Lycaeides melissa samuelis). Environmental and Ecological
Statistics, 5, 81-91.

In their abstract, these authors note "We advocate that line transect
sampling is preferable to Pollard-Yates transects as a survey technique
for monitoring Karner blue butterflies. The Pollard-Yates surveys do not
adjust for differences in site detectability. As a consequence,
estimates of among-site from Pollard-Yates surveys can be biased."

A more recent paper

Pocewicz, A., Morgan, P. & Eigenbrode, S. (2009) Local and landscape
effects on butterfly density in northern Idaho grasslands and forests.
Journal of Insect Conservation, 13, 593-601.

describes the use of line transect sampling and density estimation using
Distance.  The paper by Pocewicz et al. (2009) does a nice job of
showing the detection functions fitted to their data from 2 different
habitat types.

Download a copy of Distance 6.0, have a look at the users guide, and
especially the sample projects that come with the software, and that
should start you on your way to collecting and analysing butterfly data
in the field for analysis with distance sampling methods.

Adding to Eric's comments, for falcons, you might expect to get bias=20
from movement.  Any bias will be greater for point transect sampling=20
than line transect sampling.  (One of the assumptions of line transect=20
sampling is that any movement of animals is slow relative to the speed=20
of the observer;  point transect sampling assumes no movement.)  If most=20
birds are detected in flight, then you'll need a field protocol to deal=20
with this - see the 2001 distance sampling book, e.g. pp198-203.

Note also that 4 lines is inadequate replication to give good estimation=20
of abundance - your variance estimate will be extremely unreliable.  You=20
would be better having more shorter lines, spread through the state=20
park.  Again, see the 2001 book.

Steve Buckland

On 14/09/2010 08:08, Eric Rexstad wrote:
> > Carlos:
> >
> > All else being equal, line transect sampling is preferable to point=20
> > transect sampling if for no other reason than you are gathering data=20
> > while moving.  If there is a reason why you cannot gather data while=20
> > moving (rugged terrain, being swamped by detections, needing to=20
> > distinguish calls of multiple species) then you should use point=20
> > counts.  But there are challenges with point counts; namely the number=20
> > of animals available to be detected by you while at a point is small=20
> > near to the point and increases as distance from the point increases;=20
> > even if animals are distributed uniformly in the habitat.  This is=20
> > because of the geometry of a circle (area of a circle increases as the=20
> > square of the circle radius).

messages.subject: Site level density estimates with low occupancy
messages.subject_clean: Site level density estimates with low occupancy
messages.body_plain:
I'm using distance sampling to study the effects of several landscape fac=
tors on Northern Bobwhite densities across various sites in North Carolin=
a and South Carolina.  We surveyed 148 sites across the two states over t=
he last two summers (2009-2010).  Each site was surveyed twice during eac=
h summer.=20=20

I'm using the MCDS engine in Distance to calculate a density estimate at =
site level using the data I've collected.  In order to estimate density f=
or each site, I have essentially had to double stratify the data.  I have=
 classified the percentage forest surrounding each of my sites and classi=
fied each site into a low, medium, or high percent forest class.  I've cr=
eated a data filter in distance that selected sites that were within each=
 "% forest class".  After selecting for a particular % forest class (1,2,=
 or 3), I then post-stratified using the sample label (or by each site). =
 This essentially allowed me to estimate the density for each site but us=
e the detection probability that was calculated for each % forest class (=
or at the global level).=20=20

So, I calculated an estimate of  density for each site but the problem I'=
m running into is I'm getting really high % CVs and wide confidence inter=
vals.  Beacuase of the limited number of visits to each site, my observat=
ion numbers of bobwhites per site are low (9 being a high number of obser=
vations for a site over the two summers).  I'm pretty sure this is what i=
s causing the high % CVs and wide confidence intervals.

I've heard about some people that are using program R with a bootstrappin=
g method to help with this issue of low observations per site but have be=
en unable to track down any concrete information.

I was interesting to see if anyone else has dealt with this issue, used t=
he bootstrapping method within R or has any other suggestions on how to a=
ttempt to compensate with low numbers of observations.=20=20=20

Thanks,
Shannon Bowling
Master Student=20
North Carolina State University

messages.body_plain:
Dwight, list,

I guess you're referring to Lisa Baril's message of 12/Sept and Steve's
reply of 13/Sept.

If Lisa wants to estimate density by year and point, then she says that
some points were not surveyed in the first year, and so clearly this
will not be possible.  But this is not a problem for the subsequent
model she will be building so long as the probability of missing a point
is not correlated with the density being especially low or high, given
the habitat etc. (in other words, so long as the reason for the data
being missing is "ignorable").

(The modelling approach is outlined in the paper Steve Buckland referred
to -- I didn't see the explicit reference in his posting so here it is:
Buckland, S.T., Russell, R.E., Dickson, B.G., Saab, V.A., Gorman, D.G.
and Block, W.M. 2009.  Analysing designed experiments in distance
sampling.  Journal of Agricultural, Biological and Environmental
Statistics 14, 432-442.
and it's available here:
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/stb/buckland%20et%20al%20jabes%202009.pdf
)

If she just wants to estimate density by point, pooled across years,
then there are no points without any surveys, so it's no problem at all
(again, so long as the variation between number of visits is not related
to density).  The effort per point is the total number of visits.

I emphasize that the modelling approach is not currently available in
Distance -- such analyses need to be programmed in a stats package such
as R, which might call the distance analysis engine to calculate
detection probabilities or related quantities.  If you are stuck on how
to do this, it might be helpful to look at a report by Eric Rexstad that
gives an example of doing distance sampling analyses in R, at
  http://hdl.handle.net/10023/629
or contact Prof. Buckland for a copy of his code.  One day these things
will be available in the Distance interface, I hope!

Hope this helps,

  - Len

--

Thank you for your good discussion on point and transect sampling but my
concern is with a private contractor who has a sampling plan and then is not
able to follow it completely because a sampling staff member is sick or a
car breaks down or the weather is too rotten to see anything.  These all in
zero observations for that particular time but the zeros are misleading.  In
cancer research, Rubin and Gary King and others have developed some fairly
robust imputation methods that should help give more reliable and valid
results than if we reduce the sampling events or use zero.

I was hoping someone had used a jackknife technique or something similar to
give us an idea of how much we can impute missing values of different types
without falling off a high cliff.

Second, and not totally unrelated, is anyone looking at mimicry using
Distance-Sampling?

On 16/09/2010 09:44, Dwight Hines wrote:
>> >> Len, and others,
>> >>
> > Thank you for your good discussion on point and transect sampling but my
> > concern is with a private contractor who has a sampling plan and then is not
> > able to follow it completely because a sampling staff member is sick or a

> >
> > I was hoping someone had used a jackknife technique or something similar to
> > give us an idea of how much we can impute missing values of different types
> > without falling off a high cliff.
This seems to reflect a misunderstanding of what distance sampling
does.  If there is no effort, there is no zero in the data.  Generally,
if a line or point could not be surveyed when intended, it would be
surveyed later.  If this is not feasible, as can occur with shipboard
surveys for example, there is a gap in the effort.  That can cause
problems if for example missing effort is correlated with animal
density.  If that is thought to occur, the DSM engine of Distance can be
used to fit a spatial model for density, which does 'impute missing
values' in the sense that it gives you estimates of animal density at
locations without effort.

> > Second, and not totally unrelated, is anyone looking at mimicry using
> > Distance-Sampling?
Less cryptic comments might elicit a response!

messages.subject: What to do when stratum extent is smaller than global truncation
messages.subject_clean: What to do when stratum extent is smaller than global truncation
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have only worked with line transects so far, so this point transect
question has me stumped.

Bird point counts were made in a large group of different size vegetation
patches, each patch containing one or more point transects, depending on
size. As detection numbers per patch were often low, the sensible way to
generate patch-level density estimates seems to be to fit a global
detection function to the pooled data and then post-stratify by patch.
However, due to the varying patch sizes, there are many patches that have
a total patch radius (treating them as circular for simplicity) that is
lower than the truncation distance that was chosen (using the p>=0.1
criterion) for the global detection function. To my mind, applying this
detection function to the patch-level data in post-stratification will
result in density underestimation for these small patches, as this
function stretches to include an area that can never include sightings in
these cases (being outside the physical limits of the small vegetation
patches).

Is this concern justified? If no, why not? If yes, what might be an
appropriate way of dealing with it? Two methods came to mind:

- use a truncation distance for the global detection function that is no
larger than the smallest patch radius. This seems quite restrictive.

- as a more convoluted approach, extract the global function and manually
evaluate/integrate it for each patch such that it is only integrated out
to a distance equivalent to the patch radius. This seems daunting! :()

Hoping someone can help with this
best regards
florian weller

---

Dr Florian Weller
Center for the Study of Agriculture, Food and Environment (CSAFE)
University of Otago
Dunedin
New Zealand

messages.subject: Re: What to do when stratum extent is smaller than global
messages.subject_clean: What to do when stratum extent is smaller than global
messages.body_plain:
Florian, yes, this is a concern.  The available area for detections
increases less fast than the method assumes, so that the estimated
detection function falls more rapidly than does the true detection
function.  You can correct for this - see pp 214-216 of the 2001 intro
distance sampling book.  In your case, you would want to estimate the
e(r) function separately for each point.  This can be done without too
much difficulty, but it cannot be done in Distance.  So this may fall
into your category of daunting!

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

There is now an online bugzilla database for Distance. This allows you to=
 search for bugs which have been reported and check to see if there has b=
een any progress made on them or if there are suggested workarounds. If y=
ou discover new bugs which are not in the database there is a facility to=
 add them.

In addition to bug reporting, bugzilla provides an option to suggest any =
enhancements you would like to see in the software. To suggest an enhance=
ment proceed as if you were reporting a bug but choose "enhancement" wher=
e you are asked for the severity of the bug.

A link to the bugzilla database for Distance can be found at:

http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/bugreport.html

Laura Marshall
